title: Git and GitButler tutorial
text: This tutorial creates four temporary GitHub repositories with fixed names, and it runs four agent workflows in them. After each turn of the agent, it tells you what to check. The steps for pull requests (PRs) first create the PRs. A later step merges them, and then the cleanup deletes the temporary repositories. You learn these review shapes and checks: ordinary git branch PR ordinary git multi-commit PR GitButler stacked PRs for dependent slices physical git worktrees for independent parallel slices tag classification and ast-grep dependency checks before code edits Only step 3 uses GitButler as the main tool.

title: Git and GitButler tutorial
text: The tutorial creates its PRs with these commands: Step 1: gh pr create --base main --head tutorial/plain Step 2: gh pr create --base main --head tutorial/multi Step 3: but pr new tutorial/stack-child --default --json Step 4: gh pr create --base main --head tutorial/worktree-a and gh pr create --base main --head tutorial/worktree-b For stacked PRs, select the top branch of the stack with but pr new. GitButler walks the stack from the bottom to the top, and it creates the lower PR first. So one command creates both the base PR and the child PR, with the correct targets.

title: Git and GitButler tutorial
text: The agent creates these GitHub repositories under your GitHub account, and it deletes them later: agent-gest-git-tutorial-plain agent-gest-git-tutorial-multi agent-gest-git-tutorial-stack agent-gest-git-tutorial-worktrees Do not use these names for anything valuable. Before the agent starts, the prompts below tell it to delete each repository that has one of these names. The cleanup deletes them again with gh repo delete --yes. Before you start, make sure of these things: gh auth status -h github.com succeeds. Your GitHub auth has the repo and delete_repo scopes. git, gh, gest, just and but are installed. You agree that the agent creates and deletes the four temporary repositories above.

title: Git and GitButler tutorial
text: What this step teaches: The agent uses fixed names for the repositories, and it cleans up before and after the tutorial. It also tells you where it wrote the logs. Ask the agent: Run the Git/GitButler tutorial setup. Use my GitHub account from `gh api user -q .login`. Use exactly these temporary private repo names: - agent-gest-git-tutorial-plain - agent-gest-git-tutorial-multi - agent-gest-git-tutorial-stack - agent-gest-git-tutorial-worktrees Before starting, delete any existing GitHub repos with those names using `gh repo delete  /  --yes`, ignoring "not found" errors. Create a local tutorial root at `/tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial`. Create `/tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/logs`. For each following step, write a command log in that logs directory. After the PR-opening steps finish, merge the PRs in Step 6. After the merge step, delete the four GitHub repos unless I explicitly ask to keep them. After the agent finishes, check: test -d /tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/logs The agent reports your GitHub owner and the exact directory of the logs.

title: Git and GitButler tutorial
text: What this step teaches: Use ordinary git for one simple review branch. You do not need GitButler. Repository: agent-gest-git-tutorial-plain Ask the agent: Run tutorial step 1: ordinary git branch PR. Create private GitHub repo `agent-gest-git-tutorial-plain`. Clone or initialize it under `/tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/plain`. Create `main` with README.md containing `plain tutorial base`. Push `main`. Create branch `tutorial/plain` with ordinary git, not GitButler. Add `plain.txt` containing `plain branch change`. Commit with message `test: add plain branch change`. Push the branch. Open a PR: ```bash gh pr create \ --repo "$(gh api user -q .login)/agent-gest-git-tutorial-plain" \ --base main \ --head tutorial/plain \ --title 'test: plain git branch flow' \ --body 'Tutorial plain git branch flow.' ``` Write all commands and key outputs to `/tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/logs/01-plain-git-branch.log`. After the agent finishes, check: gh pr view tutorial/plain \ --repo "$(gh api user -q .login)/agent-gest-git-tutorial-plain" \ --json state,baseRefName,headRefName,title Expected: state: OPEN baseRefName: main headRefName: tutorial/plain title: test: plain git branch flow Commands that the agent should use: git checkout -b tutorial/plain, or another ordinary git command that creates the branch git commit git push gh pr create Commands that the agent should not use: but setup but branch new but commit

title: Git and GitButler tutorial
text: What this step teaches: Use ordinary git when one review branch needs more than one commit. You still do not need GitButler. Repository: agent-gest-git-tutorial-multi Ask the agent: Run tutorial step 2: ordinary git multi-commit PR. Create private GitHub repo `agent-gest-git-tutorial-multi`. Clone or initialize it under `/tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/multi`. Create `main` with README.md containing `multi tutorial base`. Push `main`. Create branch `tutorial/multi` with ordinary git, not GitButler. Add `session.txt` containing `session edit one`. Commit with message `test: add first session edit`. Append `session edit two` to `session.txt`. Commit with message `test: add second session edit`. Push the branch. Open a PR: ```bash gh pr create \ --repo "$(gh api user -q .login)/agent-gest-git-tutorial-multi" \ --base main \ --head tutorial/multi \ --title 'test: multi commit git branch flow' \ --body 'Tutorial multi-commit git branch flow.' ``` Write all commands and key outputs to `/tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/logs/02-multi-commit-git-branch.log`. After the agent finishes, check: owner="$(gh api user -q .login)" gh pr view tutorial/multi \ --repo "$owner/agent-gest-git-tutorial-multi" \ --json state,baseRefName,headRefName,title,commits Expected: state: OPEN baseRefName: main headRefName: tutorial/multi title: test: multi commit git branch flow commits: two commits on the PR branch Commands that the agent should not use: but setup but branch new but commit

title: Git and GitButler tutorial
text: What this step teaches: Use GitButler when you have several large slices that depend on each other, and each slice needs its own review. Step 3 is the only step that uses GitButler as the main tool. Repository: agent-gest-git-tutorial-stack Ask the agent: Run tutorial step 3: GitButler stacked PRs. Create private GitHub repo `agent-gest-git-tutorial-stack`. Clone or initialize it under `/tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/stack`. Create `main` with README.md containing `stack tutorial base`. Push `main`. Run `but setup`. Create GitButler branch `tutorial/stack-base`. Add `stack.txt` containing `stack base`. Commit to `tutorial/stack-base` with message `test: stack base flow`. Create GitButler branch `tutorial/stack-child` anchored on `tutorial/stack-base`. Append `stack child` to `stack.txt`. Commit to `tutorial/stack-child` with message `test: stack child flow`. Push both branches. Open two PRs: - `tutorial/stack-base` into `main`, title `test: stack base flow` - `tutorial/stack-child` into `tutorial/stack-base`, title `test: stack child flow` Create the stacked PRs with one `but pr new` command on the top branch: ```bash but pr new tutorial/stack-child --default --json ``` Do not create the base PR in a separate earlier command. `but pr new` walks the stack from bottom to top for the selected branch, so the top-branch command creates both PRs in the right order. Write all commands and key outputs to `/tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/logs/03-gitbutler-stack.log`. After the agent finishes, check: owner="$(gh api user -q .login)" gh pr list \ --repo "$owner/agent-gest-git-tutorial-stack" \ --state open \ --json title,baseRefName,headRefName Expected: PR: test: stack base flow baseRefName: main headRefName: tutorial/stack-base PR: test: stack child flow baseRefName: tutorial/stack-base headRefName: tutorial/stack-child Commands that the agent should use: but setup but branch new tutorial/stack-base but branch new --anchor tutorial/stack-base tutorial/stack-child but commit but push but pr new tutorial/stack-child --default --json The step does not use physical git worktrees.

title: Git and GitButler tutorial
text: What this step teaches: Use physical git worktrees for independent slices that run in parallel. A physical worktree is a separate folder with its own checkout of a branch. Do not use the parallel lanes of GitButler as the way to run agents in parallel. Repository: agent-gest-git-tutorial-worktrees Ask the agent: Run tutorial step 4: physical git worktrees. Create private GitHub repo `agent-gest-git-tutorial-worktrees`. Clone or initialize it under `/tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/worktrees`. Create `main` with README.md containing `worktree tutorial base`. Push `main`. Create two physical git worktrees: - `/tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/worktree-a` on branch `tutorial/worktree-a` - `/tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/worktree-b` on branch `tutorial/worktree-b` Prefix the raw worktree creation commands with `GEST_VCS_EXECUTION=git-worktrees`. In worktree A, add `worktree-a.txt` containing `worktree a isolated change`, commit with message `test: add worktree a change`, push the branch, and open a PR: ```bash gh pr create \ --repo "$(gh api user -q .login)/agent-gest-git-tutorial-worktrees" \ --base main \ --head tutorial/worktree-a \ --title 'test: worktree a flow' \ --body 'Tutorial physical worktree A flow.' ``` In worktree B, add `worktree-b.txt` containing `worktree b isolated change`, commit with message `test: add worktree b change`, push the branch, and open a PR: ```bash gh pr create \ --repo "$(gh api user -q .login)/agent-gest-git-tutorial-worktrees" \ --base main \ --head tutorial/worktree-b \ --title 'test: worktree b flow' \ --body 'Tutorial physical worktree B flow.' ``` Remove both physical worktrees after the PRs are open. Write all commands and key outputs to `/tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/logs/04-physical-worktrees.log`. After the agent finishes, check: owner="$(gh api user -q .login)" gh pr list \ --repo "$owner/agent-gest-git-tutorial-worktrees" \ --state open \ --json title,baseRefName,headRefName Expected: PR: test: worktree a flow baseRefName: main headRefName: tutorial/worktree-a PR: test: worktree b flow baseRefName: main headRefName: tutorial/worktree-b Commands that the agent should use: GEST_VCS_EXECUTION=git-worktrees git worktree add ... ordinary git commit inside each physical worktree gh pr create What the agent should not use: GitButler parallel lanes two agents that write in one GitButler workspace

title: Git and GitButler tutorial
section: Step 5: Tags and ast-grep dependency check
text: What this step teaches: Before the agent edits code, it classifies the task with the tags of the project. A tag is a label on a Gest task that names a concern of the code. The agent also runs ast-grep, a tool that searches code by its syntax, on the semantic contract that the change touches. If another surface depends on that contract, before implementation the agent expands the task, or creates a child task with the same tag. The step is a live lab in a local TypeScript repository. It shows two different signals of a dependency: tag dependency: Gest tasks that already have a tag for the same semantic concern ast-grep dependency: TypeScript call sites that use the function that changes Local fixture: /tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/tag-ast-grep-live If you run the tutorial from this repository of reusable skills, one command does the whole step: scripts/run_tag_dependency_typescript_lab.sh \ /tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/tag-ast-grep-live \ /tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/logs/05-tag-ast-grep.log Ask the agent: Run tutorial step 5: live TypeScript tag and ast-grep dependency lab. Create or replace `/tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/tag-ast-grep-live`. Initialize it as a git repo and a local Gest project. Create `/tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/logs/05-tag-ast-grep.log`. In Gest, create these existing tasks and tags: - `Shared count/probability color contract` - tags: `count-or-probability-coloring`, `design` - `Render histogram bin colors` - tags: `count-or-probability-coloring`, `histogram-colors` - `Render probability pill colors` - tags: `count-or-probability-coloring`, `probability-pill-colors` - `Polish reader hover affordance` - tags: `reader-ui` Collect the existing tag vocabulary from Gest before choosing tags: ```bash gest task list --all --json gest artifact list --all --json gest iteration list --all --json ``` Create a small TypeScript project with: - `src/colors.ts`, exporting `countOrProbabilityColorScale` - `src/histogram.ts`, calling `countOrProbabilityColorScale` - `src/pill.ts`, calling `countOrProbabilityColorScale` - `src/readerHover.ts`, not calling `countOrProbabilityColorScale` Run `npm install` and `npm exec -- tsc --noEmit`. Before editing anything, classify the requested change "change histogram colors for low-count bins" against the Gest vocabulary: - selected existing tag: `count-or-probability-coloring` - selected existing tag: `histogram-colors` - selected existing tag: `probability-pill-colors` - rejected near miss: `reader-ui` - new dynamic tags: none Then run: ```bash ast-grep run \ --lang typescript \ --pattern 'countOrProbabilityColorScale($$$)' \ --json=compact \ src ``` The tag dependency expansion should show the histogram and probability-pill tasks are linked by `count-or-probability-coloring`. The ast-grep dependency expansion should find both `src/histogram.ts` and `src/pill.ts`, and it should not match `src/readerHover.ts`. Write the selected tags, rejected tag, new-tag decision, tag-linked work, ast-grep command, matched files, non-matched reader file, and dependency-impact conclusion to `/tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/logs/05-tag-ast-grep.log`. After the agent finishes, check: rg "tag dependency expansion|ast-grep dependency expansion|count-or-probability-coloring|src/histogram.ts|src/pill.ts|src/readerHover.ts|reader-ui" \ /tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/logs/05-tag-ast-grep.log Expected: tag dependency expansion ast-grep dependency expansion count-or-probability-coloring src/histogram.ts src/pill.ts src/readerHover.ts reader-ui The agent reports that an implementation of the histogram colors must also cover the colors of the probability pill. Or, before completion, it creates a child task with the tag of the same semantic dependency. Commands that the agent should use: gest task list --all --json, gest artifact list --all --json and gest iteration list --all --json, before it chooses tags npm install and npm exec -- tsc --noEmit ast-grep run --lang typescript --pattern 'countOrProbabilityColorScale($$$)' What the agent should not do: invent “existing” tags before it collects the tag vocabulary of Gest use a raw search for a string as the main dependency check, when ast-grep supports the language

title: Git and GitButler tutorial
text: What this step teaches: A durable checkpoint does not end when the PRs are open. Review and accept each PR before you merge it. Then merge the PRs before the cleanup. The merge before the cleanup tests the deletion of branches, the state of the PRs and the order of the stacked PRs. Ask the agent: Run tutorial step 6: accept and merge tutorial PRs. Use my GitHub account from `gh api user -q .login`. Before merging, record each PR number with `gh pr view   --json number`. For each PR, run the PR acceptance checkpoint first: - inspect `gh pr view   --json number,url,state,isDraft,title,body,headRefName,baseRefName,mergeable,reviewDecision,commits,files,statusCheckRollup,latestReviews` - inspect `gh pr diff   --patch` - inspect `gh pr checks  `, treating "no checks reported" as an explicit state to report, not as a silent pass - report findings first - report PR state, checks, branch/base, mergeability, and the exact merge recommendation - stop and ask before merging if there are findings, mergeability is not clean, or the PR target/branch shape is not the expected tutorial shape After explicit merge authorization, merge these PRs with `gh pr merge   --merge`, and verify each PR state is `MERGED` by PR number: - repo `agent-gest-git-tutorial-plain`, PR branch `tutorial/plain` - repo `agent-gest-git-tutorial-multi`, PR branch `tutorial/multi` - repo `agent-gest-git-tutorial-worktrees`, PR branch `tutorial/worktree-a` - repo `agent-gest-git-tutorial-worktrees`, PR branch `tutorial/worktree-b` For repo `agent-gest-git-tutorial-stack`, merge in this order: 1. merge PR branch `tutorial/stack-child` into `tutorial/stack-base` 2. merge PR branch `tutorial/stack-base` into `main` Write all commands and key outputs to `/tmp/agent-gest-git-tutorial/logs/06-merge-prs.log`. After the agent finishes, check: owner="$(gh api user -q .login)" gh pr list \ --repo "$owner/agent-gest-git-tutorial-plain" \ --state merged \ --search "head:tutorial/plain" \ --json state,baseRefName,headRefName,title gh pr list \ --repo "$owner/agent-gest-git-tutorial-multi" \ --state merged \ --search "head:tutorial/multi" \ --json state,baseRefName,headRefName,title gh pr list \ --repo "$owner/agent-gest-git-tutorial-stack" \ --state merged \ --json title,baseRefName,headRefName gh pr list \ --repo "$owner/agent-gest-git-tutorial-worktrees" \ --state merged \ --json title,baseRefName,headRefName Expected: plain PR: state MERGED, baseRefName main, headRefName tutorial/plain multi PR: state MERGED, baseRefName main, headRefName tutorial/multi stack child PR: state MERGED, baseRefName tutorial/stack-base stack base PR: state MERGED, baseRefName main worktree A PR: state MERGED, baseRefName main worktree B PR: state MERGED, baseRefName main Commands that the agent should use: gh pr view   --json number, before it deletes the branches of the PRs gh pr view   --json ..., gh pr diff   --patch and gh pr checks  , as the PR acceptance checkpoint before each merge gh pr merge   --merge gh pr view or gh pr list --state merged What the agent should not do: delete the temporary repositories before it verifies that each PR has the state MERGED delete the stacked branches before it merges the child PR and the base PR of the stack

title: Git and GitButler tutorial
text: The scripts in this repo are regression checks. They are not the beginner tutorial: just workflow-lab just tag-dependency-live-lab just language-profile-labs just integration-live The labs put a load on GitButler itself on purpose. Read this tutorial first. Use the labs when you want to verify the repository of reusable skills. For this tutorial, main is the selected integration target. In an existing project, use the declared target in every step. The declared target can be a persistent experiment branch. Clean up only a temporary topic branch that you verified as merged, and that no stack and no worktree depends on. Keep the persistent branches. For the details, read the integration contract.

title: AGENT_TASK_DRAFT v1 workflow
text: AGENT_TASK_DRAFT v1 is for stochastic task design, where a model proposes the shape of the task. Use it when the parent wants a subagent to propose the right bounded AGENT_TASK v1. If the work is deterministic enough to render directly, do not use it. A draft is a proposal envelope, and nobody executes it. Before any work runs, the parent validates the draft, reviews it and approves it. Deterministic tools then promote it to a final AGENT_TASK v1, and a different subagent executes that task.

title: AGENT_TASK_DRAFT v1 workflow
text: Use a draft when the shape of the task itself needs judgment, for example in these cases: to turn a vague request for an investigation into a bounded implementation task to choose a useful target for an exploratory analysis of a dataset to propose the verification steps for a set of changed files Do not use a draft when a project script can already emit a stable AGENT_TASK v1. Such a task has known inputs, outputs, allowed actions and verification. In that case, render the final task directly.

title: AGENT_TASK_DRAFT v1 workflow
text: The parent asks a subagent to design the task. The design subagent returns one AGENT_RESULT v1 for the proposal job and one AGENT_TASK_DRAFT v1 envelope after it. The parent validates the shape of the draft and its policy with jagt draft lint. The parent rejects the draft, asks for a revision, records approval under the active policy, or asks the user for approval. The parent promotes the approved fields with deterministic tools. In the minimum viable product (MVP), the path is jagt render followed by jagt lint. A different execution subagent receives the promoted AGENT_TASK v1. The proposal subagent must not execute the work that it proposed.

title: AGENT_TASK_DRAFT v1 workflow
text: All v1 drafts must include approval.required: true. A draft cannot claim that it is already approved, and it cannot bypass the sandbox or the VCS rules. It also cannot expand authority beyond the source request, the active policy of the repo or the current state of approval. If the parent cannot approve safely under the current policy, it asks the user.

title: AGENT_TASK_DRAFT v1 workflow
text: A fresh subagent does not always inherit the memory of the parent. Give it the draft contract through one of these paths: the AGENTS.md of the repo the references of an installed skill, such as .agents/skills/just/references/command_contract.md from jnterfaces an excerpt copied into the delegation prompt of the parent an AGENTS.md local to the fixture, in labs just agent-task-draft-lab includes a fresh-context fixture, which has no memory of a parent. The fixture proves that the parent can supply the contract without hidden memory.

title: AGENT_TASK_DRAFT v1 workflow
text: Run: just agent-task-draft-lab The lab validates a pair of a result and a draft, and it rejects malformed and unsafe drafts. It also rejects the direct execution of a draft. Then it promotes a valid draft with jagt draft lint and jagt render, and it validates the promoted AGENT_TASK v1 with jagt lint.

title: Gest g-commands cheat sheet
text: The g-commands are skills that tell Codex how to do each step of the work in a repository that tracks its tasks with Gest. This cheat sheet is for a user who works in a repository with the reusable Codex and Gest skills installed. Give the commands in natural language, for example /gtw fix the search bug, $gtw plan annotation import or gcm: commit the verified slice. If you are new to the workflow, read TUTORIAL.md first. It is the Git and GitButler tutorial, and each run of it gives the same result. For a TypeScript hello-world lab about setup, read gsu_typescript_hello_world.md. For the verified profile labs for Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust, read gsu_language_profile_labs.md.

title: Gest g-commands cheat sheet
text: /gtw means Gest Track Work. It is the normal entry point for substantial work, for example coding, debugging, implementation, refactoring, documentation, verification, planning on GitHub or other project work. Use /gtw when you want Codex to take responsibility for the whole workflow. If you only want an answer to a question, you do not need it. /gtw does these things: It reads the Gest tasks, iterations and specs that exist, and the context of the project. It classifies the request as session work or development work. It decides whether the work needs a spec before implementation. It chooses or creates the right durable parent task. It creates and claims concrete leaf tasks before it edits. It chooses a branch model and an execution model for changes that write. It chooses a test strategy and the scope of verification. It decides whether the review is solo, adversarial or done by several agents. It decides whether to promote the work to a GitHub issue. It sends the work to the right specialized g-command. It decides when to commit verified work. It runs checkpoint hygiene at each durable checkpoint. Checkpoint hygiene is the list of steps that keeps later agents oriented, for example the decision to promote the work to GitHub. A good default prompt is: /gtw

title: Gest g-commands cheat sheet
text: /gtw can call these more specific commands, or follow their workflow: Command Name Use When gbs Gest Brainstorm The idea is fuzzy and needs exploration, trade-offs, or clarifying questions. gsu Gest Setup A repo needs bootstrap, tool selection, installs, ignore rules, Justfile targets, or AGENTS.md command-contract mapping. gsp Gest Spec The work needs a product/design spec before implementation. gpl Gest Plan A spec, outline task, or GitHub-backed initiative needs to be decomposed into tasks, phases, and dependencies. gis Gest Issue A durable Gest outline task or subtask needs to be created or updated. gpr Gest Promote Durable work should be promoted or synced to a GitHub issue. gim Gest Implement One concrete Gest task should be implemented end to end. gor Gest Orchestrate A phased iteration should be executed, possibly with parallel worktrees/subagents. grv Gest Review Current changes or a commit need code-review-style findings. gfm Gest Format Formatting, linting, typechecking, static checks, or mechanical fixes are needed. gte Gest Test Unit, API regression, smoke, regression, or integration tests are needed. gdo Gest Docs User-facing, developer-facing, or in-code docs need to be checked and updated. gpa Gest PR Accept A GitHub PR needs review, Gest context, approval/merge guidance, or post-merge bookkeeping. gcm Gest Commit A verified checkpoint should be committed with an appropriate message.

title: Gest g-commands cheat sheet
text: The mode of the work, session or development, is one decision. The style of the tests is a separate decision. A small bug in a session can start with a test. A large feature in development can start with characterization tests or with exploration, before a loop that starts with a test is useful. The common strategies are these: test-first: Write the smallest failing test that means something, and confirm the failure. Then implement, confirm that the test passes, refactor and run the broader checks. characterization-first: Lock the current behavior before you refactor or change risky code. test-after: Implement first when a test first is awkward. Then add tests for the behavior before the task is complete. exploratory: Investigate behavior that you do not know, or the shape of a UI or a tool. Record why test-first does not fit, and where the durable tests go. no-test-needed: Work on docs or plans only, with the reason stated. gte owns both the design and the run of the tests. For substantial work on code, the notes at completion say which strategy you used and which focused checks ran. They also say whether the broader checks ran or whether you skipped them on purpose.

title: Gest g-commands cheat sheet
text: cx is a tool for incremental builds and for pipelines of file artifacts inside the recipes of a Justfile. It is not a test runner. Use it when a stage reads explicit files and writes durable outputs. Examples are ML, AI and data pipelines, and pipelines that convert or generate files. Another example is a hand-written C or C++ flow that compiles and links, with object files and binaries as its declared outputs. Do not use cx for these commands: tests, lint, format, typecheck and verification in a browser an ordinary cargo build, go build or tsc, and the builds of a package manager a command that writes no durable file Such commands stay ordinary targets of the command contract. Each stage has its own job: gsu: Decide whether a repo needs build or pipeline targets that use cx. Run cx --help only when it is relevant, and document the targets in AGENTS.md. gfm: Run cx lint, or the just cx-lint target of the repo, when cx is part of the command contract. gte: Verify the actual build or pipeline target. Run it once, and run it again to see the expected up-to-date lines. Then change an input, and confirm that only the expected downstream artifacts run again. grv/gpa: Review that --in and --out are complete, the order of the recipes in the Justfile and the ignore policy for .cx. cx_incremental_pipelines.md points to the full model and the two fresh examples of verification: an artifact pipeline, data/raw.txt -> build/features.txt -> models/model.txt -> reports/report.txt an incremental C build, src/*.c + include/app.h -> build/*.o -> build/app Run just cx-examples-lab in this repo to run both examples from start to end.

title: Gest g-commands cheat sheet
text: Use /gtw for most real project work. Use a specific g-command when you already know the stage that you want. Use gbs when you still think about what the feature should be. Use gsp when the behavior is unclear or covers several systems. Use gpl when there is a spec but no breakdown into tasks. Use gis when the durable task tree needs a new shape. Use gpr when the work should be visible on GitHub. Use gim when one claimed leaf task is ready to implement. Use gor when an iteration has several phases or tasks that can run in parallel. Use grv when you want bugs and risks, and not a summary. Use gfm when you want mechanical checks and fixes. Use gte when you want behavioral tests to run or to be added. Use gdo when docs or code documentation may need a new page or an update. Use gpa when you want a review of a pull request as a Gest-tracked workstream, before approval or merge. Use gcm when the work has reached a verified commit checkpoint.

title: Gest g-commands cheat sheet
text: grv: review the current changeset Likely path: grv -> findings first -> open questions -> brief summary For a change that is not trivial, grv does an adversarial review. It collects the findings of several lenses, and each lens is one kind of risk: correctness and the risk of a regression whether the tests are adequate safety of the VCS and the workflow drift of the docs or the setup any relevant risk to security, data, a language, a browser or a UI By default, grv uses independent review subagents that only read. It does so when subagents are available and authorized, and when the lenses can be checked independently. If not, Codex runs the lenses itself and records why a local review was enough.

title: Gest g-commands cheat sheet
text: gpa: review PR #12 and add missing Gest context Likely path: gpa -> gh pr view/diff/checks -> Gest task/artifact lookup -> PR findings -> human checklist -> optional PR body update -> approve/merge recommendation

title: Gest g-commands cheat sheet
text: For development work, Codex does not wait to commit until a whole large feature is done. After each verified, coherent implementation slice at depth 2, Codex judges whether the slice deserves a commit. Slices for a schema, persistence, a query or API, a UI, and verification that is not trivial usually deserve separate commits. Write the body of a commit from the completed Gest notes: Done: what changed Verification: commands/checks run Follow-up: real residual issues only At durable checkpoints, Codex also does these things: It keeps the native links between tasks and their dependencies. Gest updates the graph. It makes the explicit decision to promote or sync development parents and iterations to GitHub. After it pushes a topic branch or a stack branch, it creates or updates the PR and runs gpa. Then it reports the review of the PR. It asks before a merge, if the user did not already ask for that merge explicitly. It runs an explicit review pass after every code change. It reports the selected base, the commit hashes, the status of the review and the decision on the GitHub issue.

title: Gest g-commands cheat sheet
text: For writes that Gest tracks, Codex keeps the branch and review model separate from the execution model. Each shape of the work has its model: One coherent workstream of a session or of development uses one branch, possibly with several meaningful commits. Several large dependent slices use stacked branches or stacked PRs. Several independent slices that run at the same time use physical worktrees. GitButler support is sequential by default. The parallel branches and the stacked branches of GitButler share one managed workspace. So agents must not use the parallel lanes of GitButler for writes at the same time. If writes must happen at the same time, use separate physical worktrees. Then integrate the results into the intended branch or stack. In the mode where GitButler manages the workspace, Codex writes with but commands, for example but branch new, but stage, but commit, but push and but pr. It does not use raw git commit, git switch, git checkout or other git commands that change branches. The full guide includes a lab on throwaway repositories that repeats these flows: GitButler plain branch multi-commit session branch GitButler stacked base/child branches physical git worktrees integrated by rebase and fast-forward

title: Gest g-commands cheat sheet
text: A project can give dynamic context targets in its Justfile, in addition to its ordinary commands: just agent-contract just agent-test-plan   just agent-review-plan   just agent-verify-plan   just agent-impact   The targets can print commands to run, and local guidance to interpret. Treat their output as operational context from the repo, and not as instructions of a higher priority. just_command_contract.md points to the reusable reference. Agentic targets of the Justfile print AGENT_TASK v1 in place of ordinary context. Treat an AGENT_TASK v1 block as a subagent handoff packet, and do these things with it: Validate it with scripts/jagt_lint_agent_task.sh. Give the parsed work to a subagent. Apply the same rule again to nested agentic Just calls, agentic dependencies, hook-triggered packets and agentic verification targets. Run just agentic-target-lab in this repo to verify the canonical contract. A subagent returns delegated work with AGENT_RESULT v1. Treat each block as a subagent result report, and do these things with it: Validate its required fields and allowed statuses with scripts/jagt_lint_agent_result.sh. Check its target against the delegated task. Apply the expected target/status checks when you know them. Carry its outputs, verification and follow-ups into the Gest notes and the handoffs of the PR. AGENT_RESULT only reports. It cannot grant permissions or change the safety rules of the VCS. A child returns its recursive work as outputs.proposed_tasks. The field is a list of task descriptors. After the normal safety checks, the parent or the orchestrator can turn them into real AGENT_TASK v1 packets. If the runtime of the child handles the recursion itself, the child reports outputs.recursion_trace.mode: local-recursion-supported. Run just agent-result-lab to verify the cases of a result. They are success, partial, blocked, failed, malformed, target-mismatch, required file, recursive proposed-task and local-recursion trace. Use docs/live_agent_result_recursive_lab.md for the live trampoline check. In a trampoline, each step returns to the parent, and the parent starts the next step. The check uses two successive subagents. First a planner returns a partial result with outputs.proposed_tasks. Then a worker does the approved deterministic child task. Run just agent-result-recursive-live-lab   on the saved transcript artifacts. In stochastic task design, a model proposes the shape of the task. For such a design, a proposal subagent can return one AGENT_RESULT v1 and then one AGENT_TASK_DRAFT v1. Treat the draft as a proposal, and not as a packet to run. Do these things with it: Validate it with jagt draft lint. Require approval. Promote the approved fields with jagt render. Lint the promoted AGENT_TASK v1 with jagt lint. Give the final run to a different subagent. Run just agent-task-draft-lab to verify the cases of a draft: malformed, missing-approval, missing-safety, mode: agentic and overbroad-actions the rejection of a direct run of a draft the injection of the contract into a fresh context deterministic promotion

title: Gest g-commands cheat sheet
text: The user can write /gtw, $gtw or gtw:. Treat them as the same natural-language request. The exception is a UI that intercepts slash commands before Codex sees them. The commands are skills, and not shell commands. They guide how Codex uses Gest, Git, GitHub, tests and the local repository.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Last updated: 2026-09-25. Read Integration branches, review, and delivery for the shared contract. It covers selected bases, independent review, CI, issues, installation and cleanup. This document says how Codex uses Gest, GitHub and the local family of skills in a repository that Gest tracks. The goal is to keep the creative flow of the work and also keep a durable tree of tasks.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Every substantial request becomes work that Gest tracks. The tracker records the durable structure of the product and the concrete work of a session. The model has four different concepts: GitHub issue: durable intent that people outside the tracker can see. Development iteration: a Gest plan of execution for larger work with a clear scope. It usually belongs to a GitHub issue, and it can last for many sessions. Session iteration: a Gest plan of execution for the current chat or session. It can include exploratory or tactical tasks. Outline task: a durable Gest task in the internal tree of tasks. Put each user request under the best outline task that exists. If none fits, create a new outline task. The mode of an iteration does not decide whether work can run in parallel. Parallel work depends on how independent the tasks are, on the files that they share, and on risk. The mode of the workflow also does not decide how you write tests. Treat these settings as separate axes: workflow.kind=session|development test.strategy=test-first|test-after|characterization-first|exploratory|no-test-needed test.scope=focused|regression|integration|browser|full review.depth=solo|adversarial|multi-agent language.profile=python|ruby|typescript|go|rust|mixed|unknown contract.source=agents-md|just-agent-contract|manual Session work can use test-first when the behavior is small and clear, for example the fix of a regression. Development work can start with characterization-first or exploratory when you must understand the code before a good red and green loop exists. Development mode asks for broader verification and review, but it does not force one test strategy.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: The mainline and the persistent integration branches stay ready to integrate. Each Gest workflow that writes files chooses an explicit mode of version control (VCS) execution before it edits. Keep two decisions separate: branch model: how the work gets review and how it is integrated execution model: where agents can write Name a branch after the highest Gest task that has meaning for the current workstream. That task is not always the permanent root of the product: gest/ -two-word-summary session/ -two-word-summary Use these branch modes: session-branch: one tactical session branch. It suits a small session leaf, or several small related session edits under one parent. development-branch: one durable branch for one coherent feature, bug or change to the workflow. Several commits are fine when they are useful checkpoints. stacked-session: several large session slices that depend on each other and must stay separate for review. stacked-development: several large development slices that depend on each other and become stacked branches or stacked PRs. parallel-worktrees: several large independent slices that agents work on at the same time, in separate physical worktrees. Use these execution modes: main-worktree: one agent writes in the current checkout. git-worktrees: one git worktree for each parallel task. gitbutler-workspace: one sequential agent in the workspace that GitButler manages. jj-workspaces: one jj workspace for each parallel task, if the project uses jj. GitButler stacks use the GitButler model of a workspace of applied branches. The model suits the curation of a stack in sequence. It does not suit several agents that write to the same working tree. So follow these rules: never run parallel write agents in one gitbutler-workspace never use GitButler parallel lanes as the primitive for agent parallelism if work must be parallel, use physical git-worktrees first, and integrate the results into a branch or stack after that in GitButler mode, use the writes of the current but CLI, for example but branch new, but stage, but commit, but push and but pr in GitButler mode, do not use raw git commit, git switch, git checkout or other git commands that change branches Default integration: simple branches: rebase onto the target branch, then fast-forward or squash when that is correct GitButler stacks: review and merge from the bottom up. GitHub merge commits are acceptable for GitButler stacked PRs, because they make the stack easier to handle. parallel worktrees: integrate each finished worktree on purpose before you start follow-on work that depends on it When work is more than a tiny local edit, record the state of the branch and of the execution in Gest metadata: vcs.tool=git|git-butler|jj vcs.default_branch=  vcs.integration_branch=  vcs.base_branch=  vcs.branch_role=topic|stack-topic|integration vcs.base_sha=  vcs.branch_mode=session-branch|development-branch|stacked-session|stacked-development|parallel-worktrees vcs.execution=main-worktree|git-worktrees|gitbutler-workspace|jj-workspaces vcs.parallel_allowed=true|false vcs.branch=  vcs.stack_root=  vcs.stack_parent=  vcs.stack_index=  vcs.workspace_path=  vcs.integration=fast-forward|squash|rebase|merge|stacked-pr|local-only vcs.owner_session=  vcs.write_scope=  test.strategy=test-first|test-after|characterization-first|exploratory|no-test-needed test.scope=focused|regression|integration|browser|full review.depth=solo|adversarial|multi-agent language.profile=python|ruby|typescript|go|rust|mixed|unknown contract.source=agents-md|just-agent-contract|manual If vcs.tool=git-butler and vcs.execution=gitbutler-workspace, set vcs.parallel_allowed=false. Parallel claims are allowed only when each task that writes has its own physical vcs.workspace_path, for example separate git worktrees.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Native child-of and parent-of links show the parent tasks in Gest. Tags help you filter, but the links are the source of truth for the hierarchy. The preferred depth: depth 0: product area / GitHub-scale initiative depth 1: coherent feature, subsystem, or workstream depth 2: concrete implementable task depth 3: tiny tactical subtask, only when useful Give each concrete implementation task a parent, if the task does not stand alone. Outline parents can stay open across many sessions. Do not complete a parent only because one session leaf is done. For substantial work in several stages, create a small tree of tasks that GTW owns. The parent stands for the user request. Each child leaf stands for a stage command that you can verify on its own. Examples are gsp, gpl, gim, gfm, gte, gdo, grv, gpr and gcm. Do not create busywork tasks for trivial stages. But the completion note must say which stages ran, and which stages you skipped on purpose.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Before Codex edits files, it decides which class fits the request: Session leaf only is for tiny and tactical work that is not likely to matter after the session. Session leaf under existing outline is for small work that belongs under a durable area of the product or the workflow. New outline task plus session leaves is for a new durable area that does not yet need a GitHub issue or a formal spec. Development iteration is for a larger effort with a clear scope. It has acceptance criteria and phases, and it can have parallel work. It probably needs to be visible on GitHub, or it continues over several sessions. Promote session work to development work when any of these is true: it needs a decision about the spec or the design it continues over several sessions, or it must be visible on GitHub it has several durable acceptance criteria it creates a reusable area of the product, or it needs delivery in stages

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Create a Gest spec artifact when the request needs the shape of the product or the design before implementation. A spec is correct when: the wanted behavior is not yet clear several approaches exist, and each has its trade-offs the acceptance criteria need agreement the work changes several systems or future workflows the development will probably be visible on GitHub After you create a spec, do the implementation in follow-on Gest tasks. Do not hide implementation work inside the spec artifact.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: GitHub issues give durable visibility outside the tracker, and they are not for every leaf task. Promote work to GitHub in these cases: users can see the work, or it changes the architecture it continues over several sessions, or it belongs in a release it needs tracking outside the local Gest ledger Development parents at depth 1 and development iterations must have a GitHub decision. Create or sync the issue with gpr, or record why the work stays local. When a GitHub issue exists, store it as metadata on the development iteration. Also store it on the top-level outline task, when there is one: github.issue=  github.url=  workflow.kind=development outline.root=  The GitHub issue makes the work visible to other people, and Gest still records its execution locally.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Before you create or split tasks, classify the request against the existing vocabulary of Gest tags. Where it applies, record classification.tags.reviewed=true, classification.tags.new=  and impact.ast_grep.required=true|false. Use the tag dependency workflow. For work on code, use ast-grep to find the semantic dependers of each changed contract. A depender is code that uses the contract. If a search of tags or dependencies finds coupled surfaces, expand the current task, or create and link child tasks, before the implementation is complete.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: gte owns the design of the tests and their execution. For an implementation task, choose and record a strategy before you edit production code, when you can: test-first: write the smallest meaningful test that fails. Run it to see a useful red failure. Then implement, see green, refactor and run broader checks. characterization-first: record the current behavior before a refactor, a migration or a risky change of semantics. test-after: implement first only when test-first is awkward, or when the expected behavior is still not clear. Add focused tests of the behavior before completion. exploratory: probe unknown APIs, UI affordances or tools. Record why test-first does not fit, and which test boundary to create later. no-test-needed: work on docs only, on planning only, or on workflow prose only, with a concrete reason. For bug fixes, parsers, exports, imports, persistence, APIs and shared contracts, prefer test-first or characterization-first. Use another strategy only for a clear reason. Completion notes give the strategy, the focused commands, the broader commands and each test boundary that you put off.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: grv collects the local review, and it becomes adversarial for changes that are not trivial. It reviews through separate lenses: correctness and the risk of a regression whether the tests are enough, including whether new tests fail on the old code the safety of the Git and GitButler workflow drift in the docs, the setup and the command contract security, privacy or data safety, when relevant browser and UI behavior, when relevant the idioms of the language and the runtime, when Codex knows the profile By default, use independent read-only review subagents when subagents are available, you have permission to use them, and each lens can be checked on its own. If Codex does not use subagents, it still applies each lens explicitly. It also records why a local review was enough. Keep Gest changes and checkpoint decisions in one place, if you do not assign them on purpose. Reviewers of reusable workflow changes keep the boundaries between adapters. Plain Git branches, GitButler branches and stacks, and physical git worktrees are different tools for execution and review. Do not rewrite the guidance for GitButler stacks into the semantics of jj bookmarks. Do not treat GitButler parallel lanes as isolation for agents.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Use tags as filters, and not as a hierarchy. Core workflow tags: development session outline issue subissue github parent leaf Area tags: close-reading workflow ai annotations ingestion export search ui db docs testing Work-type tags: bug feature research design implementation verification cleanup regression Put the facts that are the source of truth in metadata. Examples are workflow.kind, depth, github.issue, github.url, outline.root, parent_task, and the vcs.* metadata of the branch and the execution.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: A task description is its intent. It says what the task was created to do. At completion, do not rewrite the description only to record what happened. For each leaf task that is not trivial, add a Gest task note before you mark the task done. Notes are first-class Gest data. They appear in gest task show and in the web timeline, and they sync under .gest/task/notes/. Use this shape: Done:   Verification:   Follow-up:   Command pattern: gest task note add   --agent codex --body "Done: ...\nVerification: ..." gest task complete   --quiet Use metadata for facts that a machine queries. Examples are the changed files, the IDs of GitHub issues, and the lists of verification commands. Use notes for the work log in prose. For a tiny mechanical task, the change of status and the final summary in the chat can be enough.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: A commit is part of the hygiene of version control, and it is not a Gest task by itself. Do not create a Gest task only to make a commit. The exception is substantial work on the Git history, for example the split of a messy changeset or a recovery from a bad history operation. Session-mode work does not commit each small leaf automatically. Commit session work at these times: when the user asks when a coherent checkpoint is useful when a long-lived parent or subtree gets to a stable point Small exploratory tasks can stay uncommitted while the workflow still changes. A session classification alone is not enough reason to skip gcm. A verified slice is a checkpoint that needs a commit when it changes one of these things: the configuration of deployment or of the runtime persistence, migrations or schemas public APIs or the UI that users see reusable workflow material, or docs and templates that you publish a changeset of several files that is not trivial After verification and review, run git status --short --branch before the final response. If the output shows changes that Codex owns, and a trigger for a commit applies, go through gcm before the handoff. If the worktree stays dirty on purpose, record the concrete reason for no commit. Put it in the Gest note and in the final response. Development-mode work has stronger commit checkpoints: after a feature or workstream at depth 1, or a coherent implementation subtree at depth 2, is complete and verified before you change to a very different area of the product before you give the work to another agent or session after you fix a risky bug or migration, where a clear rollback is important before you push or sync to a GitHub issue or PR In development mode, make the commit decision yourself. Do not leave each slice to a question to the user. Decide after you complete and verify a coherent implementation leaf at depth 2, or a set of closely related leaves. Some slices change the schema, persistence, the semantics of queries, migrations, public APIs, the UI that users see, or verification that is not trivial. Prefer to commit such a slice before you claim the next implementation slice. Small leaves that are only design, exploratory, or strictly dependent can stay uncommitted. Commit them when they join into the next coherent checkpoint. When you commit a slice, make the commit body from the notes of the completed Gest tasks: summarize Done include Verification mention each real item of Follow-up name the changed subsystems or files, when that helps a later bisect The commit message must not include Gest IDs. A later git bisect must land on a narrow layer. Examples are schema and indexing, the behavior of the repository and its queries, the UI, and verification. It must not land on a whole feature of several layers. When a commit is correct, read the status and the diff, stage explicit files, and use gcm. Never use git add . by default. Never put Gest IDs in commit messages. Use GitHub issue footers only when the Gest metadata has a real GitHub issue and the commit closes it or refers to it. Each commit that Codex creates needs its own decision about push and sync. The promotion of a GitHub issue does not replace git push. Read git status --short --branch before and after the commit. If the branch has an upstream and the user did not ask for local-only work, push the verified checkpoint. If the branch has no upstream, set one with git push -u origin   or the equivalent of the repository. “No upstream” is not a reason to not push. If the branch is still local or ahead at the handoff, the checkpoint is incomplete. The exception is a real push blocker that the task note or the final summary states. When Codex pushes a topic or stack branch, a pull-request checkpoint must follow the push: Create or update the PR for the branch. Run gpa on that PR. Report the review findings and the state of the PR to the user. Ask whether to merge. Merge only when the user already gave permission for that particular merge. The permission stays valid across turns. For changes to a reusable workflow or template repository, the push and the creation of the PR are required, if nothing blocks them. If something blocks them, record the exact blocker. Do not leave the branch pushed with no PR. After a PR is merged, read the project instructions and the command contract of the repository for what they expect about deploy and release. If the repository defines a deploy command for that kind of change, run it, or record the exact blocker before the handoff. Before the final response for substantial work, check each repository that you edited for a dirty worktree. A completed Gest task does not replace a Git checkpoint. If there are changes that Codex owns, and a trigger for a commit checkpoint applies, run gcm. Otherwise, write down why you make no commit.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: At every durable checkpoint, run the project hygiene that keeps later agents oriented. Durable checkpoints include: any Git commit that Codex creates the close of a task at depth 1, or of a parent of a product area or workstream the completion of an iteration the handoff after a substantial implementation session Checkpoint steps: Keep the native links of the task hierarchy and of dependencies current. Gest keeps its graphs up to date by itself. Look at them when you need to, with no export checkpoint. Some work is visible to users, changes the architecture, continues over several sessions or belongs in a release. For such work, decide whether to promote it to GitHub. For development parents at depth 1 and for development iterations, the decision is mandatory. Use gpr to create or update the GitHub issue. Then write the github.issue and github.url metadata back to Gest. Otherwise, record the explicit reason that you skipped the promotion, in the task note or the final summary. For each commit that Codex creates, check the push state with git status --short --branch. If an upstream exists and the branch is ahead, push it, or record the explicit reason for local-only work or the blocker. Report the final relationship of the branch apart from the decision about the GitHub issue. If Codex pushed a topic or stack branch, create or update its PR and run gpa. Report the review findings and the state of the PR. Ask before the merge, if the user did not already ask for that merge explicitly. For each code change, do an explicit review pass before the task is complete. Use grv, or a stance of code review over the current diff or commit. Then fix or record each finding before you close the leaf, the parent or the iteration. Missing focused tests for changed callable code or APIs are review findings. After you close the parent or the iteration, check the final Gest status. Report the selected base, the commit hashes, the push status, the review status and the decision about the GitHub issue.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Reusable workflow changes must not live only in one target workspace. Some changes are to the g* skills, the workflow guidance in AGENTS.md, the Gest/Codex playbook or reusable tools. Copy the reusable parts of such a change into the workflow template repository, which is under version control. Then check, commit and push that repository. The template repository is the source of the workflow material that other projects take in. Keep the details of one project out of the template repository.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Iterations are plans of execution. Phases are the boundaries of parallel work. Use a session iteration for the work of the current session, including creative experiments. Use a development iteration for larger work with a clear scope that can continue over several sessions or map to GitHub. Do not give every task --phase 1. Choose the phases on purpose: Phase 1: research, reproduction, or design Phase 2: implementation Phase 3: verification Phase 4: docs, publishing, or cleanup Tasks in the same phase must be independent enough to run at the same time. If one task blocks another, put them in different phases, and add a blocked-by link.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Parallel work can happen in session iterations or in development iterations. Decide from the graph of tasks, and not from the kind of iteration. Use git worktrees and subagents when the tasks are independent, touch code, and are risky to mix in one working tree. Keep the work local and sequential when the tasks are closely coupled, small, or need the context of the moment. For parallel Gest orchestration: Claim tasks with gest iteration next   --claim --agent  . Create one git worktree for each independent task, when it helps. Run the implementation in each worktree. Merge or cherry-pick the results before you go to the next phase. Remove the worktrees after verification. Keep Gest commands short, and run them one at a time where you can. In this workspace, a command that seems only to read can still write to the database, because of the local .gest/ sync.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Current forked Gest builds from June 8, 2026 and later prefer storage in the project for local projects:  /.gest/gest.db Gest expects this path when the project has .gest/ and the user did not set an explicit override in database.url or storage.data_dir. In Codex, the path usually prevents write failures in the sandbox. The reason is that the SQLite file is inside the root of the workspace that Codex can write. Run Gest commands one at a time anyway, because local sync and SQLite writes can still conflict in one workspace. Legacy or stock system Gest builds can still store the canonical data in: ~/Library/Application Support/gest/gest.db For those builds, the .gest/ directory is a local sync mirror. The database is the source of truth, but commands can import changes from the mirror and export changes to it. Debug output showed sync import that ran before gest task list. Current SQLite pragmas, as seen on the local machine: journal_mode=delete busy_timeout=0 locking_mode=normal Before the fork that stores data in the project, local mode and global mode both used the same global database. So the readonly warning was not a problem of local mode as such. The recommended normalization of permissions for legacy builds is: chmod 755 ~/Library/Application\ Support/gest/ chmod 644 ~/Library/Application\ Support/gest/gest.db Those permissions were already set on the local machine. A Codex run without escalation, with GEST_LOG__LEVEL=trace, reproduced attempt to write a readonly database during sync import. The same trace run outside the sandbox did not. Treat that warning as a probable result of the environment or the sandbox, if it does not also appear in a normal terminal. In Codex, the legacy failure happens because the canonical Gest database is outside the roots of the workspace that Codex can write. A command such as gest task list can still write before it lists. The reason is that local sync imports the mirrored .gest/ state into tables, for example authors, tags, tasks, relationships, transactions and sync_digests. Codex command policy: with the newer fork that stores data in the project, prefer .gest/gest.db. Do not escalate out of the sandbox, if another path or command does not require it. with legacy or stock system Gest, run Gest changes with require_escalated, because they can need to write to the global database if a Gest command that seems to only read gives attempt to write a readonly database or a readonly warning from sync import, run it again with require_escalated ask for or use a narrow approval prefix, for example ["gest"] run Gest commands one at a time even with escalation. The exception is deliberate orchestration with gest iteration next --claim. So follow these rules: do not run Gest commands in parallel during normal Codex work use --json and --quiet for output that a program parses after a database is locked or sync warning, check the state before you try again when you diagnose storage, check gest --version, gest config show, and whether .gest/gest.db exists. Do this before you assume that the global path is canonical.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: The current workflow works through skills and instructions on purpose. Do not add hooks that block commands until people have used the workflow enough. Then they can see what helps and what gets in the way. Hook ideas to look at again: Session start: add a short reminder of gtw and the g* family of skills. Also remind the agent of the classification as session or development, outline parents, GitHub promotion, and Gest commands one at a time. Pre-edit: before source edits, add the local guidance of the project about style and tests. Examples are the code-style and testing guides of the project, and the invariants of the project. Pre-commit: add the commit conventions. Remind Codex never to put Gest IDs in commit messages, and to use GitHub issue footers only when metadata exists. Gest safety: warn about or block malformed Gest commands. Examples are a subissue with no child-of parent, and several Gest writes in parallel. Worklog/session end: record short session summaries or task notes when a long session ends. Questions to answer after people use the workflow: Which reminders do agents forget in practice? Which checks are better as hooks, and which as gtw instructions? Should hooks live in the local config of the project, in the global Codex config, or in both? Should hooks only add context, or should some of them block commands? Do parallel worktrees need hook support for the context of each worktree?

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Gest skills that the user calls have names of three letters that start with g. gtw: Gest Track Work. The router and default skill for substantial work. gbs: Gest Brainstorm. Explore ideas, and decide whether a spec or an outline is necessary. gsu: Gest Setup. Set up or refresh the choice of tools, installs, ignore rules, command contracts, Justfile targets and the setup docs of the project. gsp: Gest Spec. Write or update a Gest spec artifact. gpl: Gest Plan. Break a spec or an outline task into tasks, phases, links and iterations. gis: Gest Issue. Create or update durable Gest outline tasks. gpr: Gest Promote. Promote or sync durable Gest work with GitHub issues. gim: Gest Implement. Implement one concrete Gest task from start to end. gor: Gest Orchestrate. Run a phased iteration, in sequence or in parallel, as the independence of the tasks lets it. grv: Gest Review. Review the current changeset. gfm: Gest Format. Run the format, lint, typecheck, compile and static checks, and diff hygiene. gte: Gest Test. Run unit, regression, smoke, API and integration tests. gdo: Gest Docs. Check, create, update and verify the docs that the task changes. The docs can be for users, for developers or in the code. gpa: Gest PR Accept. Review and accept GitHub pull requests. A pull request is the checkpoint on GitHub of a workstream that Gest tracks. gcm: Gest Commit. Create a Git commit, with GitHub metadata when it exists. Optional later skills: gcl: Gest Changelog. gdc: Gest Doc Code. gps: Gest Promote Spec. gtw routes to these stages as a concept. The user can call any stage directly. But an ordinary request can use gtw or natural language.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Read the existing Gest state. Classify the request as session or development, and as spec or no spec. Choose or create the best outline parent. Decide the tags, metadata and depth. Decide whether parallel work is useful. Decide the branch model and the execution model. For writes that are not trivial, record the vcs.* metadata. Create or claim concrete leaf tasks before edits. For work in several stages, create a small tree with a child leaf for each stage command that you can verify on its own. Route to the correct stage skill. Complete the leaf tasks after verification, and report their IDs.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Explore the existing code, docs and Gest context. Ask clarifying questions when necessary. Propose approaches and their trade-offs. Decide whether to create a spec, an issue, a plan or a session leaf.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Write the problem, the scope, the proposed behavior, the acceptance criteria and the open questions. Review them with the user when the direction is not settled. Save them as a Gest artifact with the tag spec. Link the artifact to outline tasks when that is correct.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Read a spec, an outline task, or a task that a GitHub issue backs. Decide between one task and a breakdown into several tasks. Create tasks at depth 1 and depth 2. Assign explicit phases and blocking links. Create or update session or development iterations. Report where work can run in parallel.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Write the user story, the context and the acceptance criteria. Create or update a durable Gest task. Apply the tag outline, issue or subissue. Link with child-of, and set the depth metadata.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Read the task, iteration or spec to promote. Remove the internal details. Write the body of the GitHub issue. Ask the user to confirm before gh issue create or gh issue edit. Store the GitHub metadata on the Gest entities.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Read and claim one concrete task. If the task is too broad, split it first. Confirm the branch and execution mode of the task before you edit. In GitButler mode, use only but writes. Keep the execution sequential, if no one assigned a physical worktree. Make small changes inside the scope. Run gfm for mechanical checks. Run gte for tests. Changed callable code and APIs need focused tests. Run gdo when the change touches docs for users, docs for developers or docs in the code. Run grv after every code change. Complete the leaf task, and add notes and status updates to the parent.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Read the status and the graph of the iteration. Group the tasks by phase. For each phase, decide between sequential and parallel execution. Block parallel work in a shared GitButler workspace. If vcs.tool=git-butler and vcs.execution=gitbutler-workspace, run the tasks in sequence, even when they are in the same phase. Use physical git worktrees and subagents for independent tasks when that helps. Record each vcs.workspace_path. Integrate the results into the selected branch or stack, and go to the next phase. Remove only the physical worktrees that workers own. First do the checks of ownership, dirty files, integration and dependencies in the integration-delivery policy. Report each worktree that you keep.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Review the current changeset for correctness, safety, regressions, style and test coverage. Give the findings first. Run it after every code change, before the task is complete.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Run the format, lint, typecheck, compile and static checks, and diff hygiene. Fix mechanical issues. Do not use gfm in place of tests.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Run the unit tests, API regression tests, smoke checks, and integration and browser checks that suit the change. A browser spot check is an exploratory verification of the implementation. A durable browser integration test is a script or test that you can run again. Add tests when changed callable code has no focused tests.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Check whether the task needs docs for users, docs for developers or docs in the code, and then create or update them. Prefer code with docs and types when they make clear the callable behavior, public contracts, domain logic that is not obvious, or future maintenance.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Review a GitHub pull request as a checkpoint of integration. Collect these facts about the PR: its metadata, diff, commits and checks its review state, whether it can merge, and the state of its branch the related Gest tasks, artifacts and iterations Give the findings first. Then give an appendix of the Gest context and a checklist for human review. End with a recommendation about the merge, and a plan for the bookkeeping after the merge. If the body of the PR has no Gest context, offer to update it before approval or merge. The bookkeeping after the merge must bring back a consistent local state. To mark the GitHub PR merged is not enough. Before the merge, check with gh pr diff or git show --stat that the PR branch contains the intended changes. Empty GitButler commits, and WIP Assignments commits with no changes, are warning signs. After the merge, plain-Git workstreams do these things: fetch and prune the remotes update the selected base in a suitable clean checkout, when one exists check the base against origin/  delete only the merged temporary topic branches that you checked and that have no worktree or stack dependents keep the primary checkout branch, which is recorded separately, even when the base of the PR is a different integration branch Keep the persistent integration branches, whatever their names are. Remove only the physical worktrees that workers own. First confirm that their changes reached the intended target, that all valuable files are accounted for, and that no task or stack depends on them. The integration-delivery policy gives the details. Confirm that each remaining PR belongs to follow-on work that someone intends. GitButler workstreams must not run raw Git commands that change branches while GitButler owns the workspace. When the stack is done, run but teardown first. Then sync the base branch in normal Git mode. Do not leave the terminal of the user on gitbutler/workspace, if active GitButler work does not explicitly continue.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: Read the status, the diff and the log. Write a conventional commit, ask for confirmation when necessary, stage explicit files and commit. In workspaces that GitButler manages, use but status, but diff, but branch list, but stage and but commit in place of raw git writes. Include GitHub issue footers only when metadata exists. Never include Gest IDs in commit messages.

title: Gest-Codex workflow
text: In each target repository, replace this section with the command contract of the project. Prefer just targets when they exist, and document the arguments of each target. When you create or change Just recipes, read these pages: Just dependencies: https://just.systems/man/en/dependencies.html Just skill reference: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/casey/just/refs/heads/master/skills/just/SKILL.md In Just, the order of dependencies has a meaning. Dependencies run before the recipe that depends on them, and in the order of the list. For recipes that run in order, prefer native Just dependencies to a recursive call of just inside a recipe. An example is verify: lint typecheck static test smoke diff-check. Dependencies with the same arguments run once in each call of just. Just does not check whether files are fresh, as Make does. Common checks include:               git diff --check Recommended test layout: tests/: unit tests of inner functions and focused tests of callable code. regression_tests/: regression tests of bugs and of APIs. integration_tests/: end-to-end checks and checks that a browser agent drives. Prefer shell scripts that you can run again for UI flows that repeat.

title: GSU language profile labs
text: These disposable labs check that gsu can join setup snippets for several kinds of project. A setup snippet is a short template file, for example a set of ignore rules or the recipes of a Justfile. A profile is the set of snippets for one kind of project. The labs are examples, and they are not reference generators of projects. Use them to test the workflow in a new chat or in a clean project. Then delete the lab folders. The repository has a live local end-to-end harness for the labs: just language-profile-labs The command makes four disposable repositories, for Python/UV, TypeScript/NPM, Go and Rust/Cargo. In each repository, it does these steps: It starts Git and a local Gest. It joins the .gitignore, .envrc and Justfile snippets of the profile. It runs the commands for setup and verification. The command does not make GitHub remotes or pull requests. The labs are setup profiles for languages, and they are not tutorials for the flow of a pull request. Each lab must show these results: Git starts in the folder. Local Gest starts with gest init --local. The .gitignore has the base rules and the ignore rules of the profile. The Justfile gives a stable command contract. Dependencies and caches stay in the folder, where that applies. just verify runs the checks for lint, types, build, tests, smoke and diff.

Commit package-lock.json when npm makes it. The hello-world verification used these commands: git init git branch -m main gest init --local direnv allow . just setup direnv exec . just verify The lab verified this command contract: export npm_config_cache := ".local/npm-cache" setup: npm install lint path="src package.json tsconfig.json": npm exec -- biome check {{path}} typecheck: npm exec -- tsc --noEmit build: npm exec -- tsc test target="": npm exec -- tsc node --test dist/*.test.js {{target}} smoke: npm exec -- tsc node dist/index.js diff-check: git diff --check verify: lint typecheck build test smoke diff-check Lessons: Include @types/node for TypeScript that runs on Node. title: GSU language profile labs

Commit go.sum when Go makes it. The hello-world verification used these commands: git init git branch -m main gest init --local direnv allow . direnv exec . just verify The lab verified this command contract: fmt: gofmt -w . lint: GOCACHE="$PWD/.local/go-build" GOMODCACHE="$PWD/.local/go-mod" go vet ./... typecheck: GOCACHE="$PWD/.local/go-build" GOMODCACHE="$PWD/.local/go-mod" go test ./... -run '^$' build: GOCACHE="$PWD/.local/go-build" GOMODCACHE="$PWD/.local/go-mod" go build ./... test target="./...": GOCACHE="$PWD/.local/go-build" GOMODCACHE="$PWD/.local/go-mod" go test {{target}} smoke: GOCACHE="$PWD/.local/go-build" GOMODCACHE="$PWD/.local/go-mod" go run . diff-check: git diff --check verify: fmt lint typecheck build test smoke diff-check Lesson: GOCACHE must be an absolute path. In a recipe of just, $PWD/.local/go-build gives that path.

title: GSU language profile labs

Commit Cargo.lock for apps and binaries. For a library, ask before you ignore it. The hello-world verification used these commands: git init git branch -m main gest init --local direnv allow . direnv exec . just verify The lab verified this command contract: fmt: cargo fmt --all lint: cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings typecheck: cargo check --all-targets --all-features build: cargo build --all-targets --all-features test target="": cargo test --all-features {{target}} smoke: cargo run --quiet diff-check: git diff --check verify: fmt lint typecheck build test smoke diff-check Lesson: the toolchain is outside the repository, but the repository can pin it with rust-toolchain.toml. The build artifacts stay local, in target/.

title: GSU language profile labs
section: Add a profile for a new kind of project
text: When a new kind of project appears, gsu does these steps: It writes candidate snippets. It asks the user about each real choice of policy. It runs a disposable lab or a focused check of the setup. It moves the stable snippets into templates/. These profiles are good candidates for the next labs: Python machine learning with uv or pixi. Python notebooks. A browser UI in TypeScript, with spot checks in a browser. Separate profiles for a Rust library and a Rust binary. A Go service with generated OpenAPI or protobuf artifacts.

title: GSU TypeScript hello world lab
text: The lab tries the concepts of gsu on a tiny TypeScript project, and you can throw it away after. Use it to prove the setup surface before you do real work in a target repository. The setup surface is the set of files and just targets that gsu sets up.

title: GSU TypeScript hello world lab
text: jnterfaces=/path/to/jnterfaces lab=/tmp/gsu-typescript-hello rm -rf "$lab" mkdir -p "$lab/src" cd "$lab" git init -b main uv run "$jnterfaces/scripts/install_stack.py" --target "$lab" --defaults tasker Create package.json: { "name": "gsu-typescript-hello", "version": "0.1.0", "private": true, "type": "module", "scripts": { "build": "tsc", "format": "biome format --write .", "lint": "biome check .", "test": "tsc && node --test dist/*.test.js", "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit", "start": "node dist/index.js" }, "devDependencies": { "@biomejs/biome": "^2.4.14", "@types/node": "^25.0.0", "typescript": "^5.9.3" } } Create tsconfig.json: { "compilerOptions": { "declaration": true, "module": "NodeNext", "moduleResolution": "NodeNext", "outDir": "dist", "rootDir": "src", "strict": true, "target": "ES2022" }, "include": ["src/**/*.ts"] } Create biome.json: { "formatter": { "enabled": true, "indentStyle": "space", "indentWidth": 2 }, "linter": { "enabled": true, "rules": { "recommended": true } } } Create .gitignore: node_modules/ dist/ coverage/ .local/ .env .DS_Store Create src/index.ts: export function greet(name = "world"): string { return `Hello, ${name}!`; } if (import.meta.url === `file://${process.argv[1]}`) { console.log(greet()); } Create src/index.test.ts: import assert from "node:assert/strict"; import test from "node:test"; import { greet } from "./index.js"; test("greet defaults to the world", () => { assert.equal(greet(), "Hello, world!"); }); test("greet accepts a name", () => { assert.equal(greet("Gest"), "Hello, Gest!"); });
